headline: Boulder fields holding peanuts, stripers going deep — Watch Hill corridor is the one to watch
subhead: Bait is stacking on the rock piles from Ram Island to Wamphassuc, but the albies haven't crossed the line yet — the new moon on the 12th is the trigger everybody's circling.
body_markdown:
First light off Ram Island Wednesday, and the water over the boulder field was nervous before I even cut the engine. Peanut bunker, balled tight, pushed up against the granite in maybe six feet of water, flickering like a school of minnows trying to disappear into the rock itself. That's the tell this time of year — when the bait starts hugging structure instead of running open water, something's pushing it. I poled the skiff along the edge, quiet, watching for the boil that didn't come. Not yet. But the bait knows something's coming before we do, and right now it's balling up tight against every rock pile from Ram Island down through the Wicopesset Passage.

The striper pattern out here hasn't changed much from what I was seeing a week ago, and that's not surprising — I said then that this holding pattern would run until the tide started building into the new moon, and that's exactly where we are. Fish are deep, they're feeding at night and on the edges of light, and they're not showing themselves on top the way they will once that current really starts moving. Kings Point is reading close to 71 degrees, New London's a little cooler at 69.4, and that gradient matters — the eastern Sound stays a touch behind the western Sound all summer, which is part of why our albie window always opens a beat later than Long Island's. Right now that cooler water is holding stripers down on the structure rather than pushing them up to chase.

Best bass action has come off Wamphassuc Point and the boulder field east of Esker Point, fished on the last two hours of the outgoing into dead low, working eels and jointed swimmers — Red Fins and Bombers in the darker colors — slow and deep along the rock edges. A few fish to 30 inches came off Wamphassuc on live eels fished at night, drifted with just enough weight to keep them ticking the bottom without hanging up in the boulders, which out here is its own skill. You lose gear on this bottom if you're not paying attention to the drift speed. I've buried more bucktails in Fishers Island Sound rock than I care to count, and I still do it.

The Stonington breakwater has been steadier than the open rock piles, especially on the slack tide change, which is when the current stops fighting you and you can actually work a jig down into the rocks without snagging every other cast. Fluke have been mixed in there too, along the sand pockets between the rip-rap, mostly on white Gulp swimming mullets tipped with squid strips, fished tight to the base of the breakwater on the last of the flood. Nothing huge — most going 16 to 19 inches — but enough keepers mixed in to make the stops worthwhile if you're patient with the drift.

Black sea bass are still cooperating on the deeper structure out toward Fishers Island — the rock piles and scattered boulder fields off the north side hold them well into August, and small pieces of clam or squid on a simple two-hook bottom rig will produce steadily in 20 to 35 feet. It's not glamorous fishing but it fills a cooler while you wait on the bigger story developing to our east.

And that story is the bonito and albie push working through the Watch Hill corridor. I've had my eye on that warm current line for two weeks now, the way it runs off Watch Hill and pushes bait through the rips toward Sandy Point and into Little Narragansett Bay. We flagged this pattern last week — said the building tide into the August 12 new moon would be the trigger that sharpens the current-driven bite and likely brings the first albies and bonito into range at Montauk, Block Island, and the eastern Sound. Nothing confirmed yet on this side of the line — no hookups, no boils reported off Napatree or the Watch Hill reef — but the ingredients are all there. Bait's staging, the current is about to load up harder with the new moon four days out, and that corridor runs straight into our water.

If I had one day this week, I'd spend the early morning working the boulder fields with the fly rod — small Deceivers and Clouser minnows worked slow along structure edges for stripers while the light's low — and I'd keep a rod rigged with a small metal, a half-ounce epoxy jig or a Deadly Dick, ready to go the second I see a nervous patch of water or a bird working tight over bait near Sandy Point or the Wicopesset rips. That's how the albie bite starts out here — not with a blitz, but with one bird, one boil, and if you're not already rigged you miss it.

By this weekend, with the tide building harder into the 12th, I expect the striper bite to sharpen on the structure — moving current always wakes up the boulder fields — and I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first albie report cross the line from Watch Hill into our water by early next week. Worth checking the rips daily starting now. Just don't expect fireworks yet. Right now it's still bait and patience, watching the rocks, waiting for the water to tell you it's time.
